name: Pioneer 10
why: The first spacecraft to cross the asteroid belt and visit Jupiter, it is now coasting out of the solar system with no power left to call home.
science: Pioneer 10 took the first close-up pictures of Jupiter in December 1973 and measured its fierce radiation belts. It proved that spacecraft could safely fly through the asteroid belt.
story: I was the first to sail through the asteroid belt and the first to visit Jupiter. I kept talking to Earth for more than 30 years, until my last faint whisper arrived in January 2003. Now I glide silently in the direction of Aldebaran, the red star that marks the eye of Taurus the Bull.
funFact: Pioneer 10 carries a plaque with drawings of a man, a woman and a map showing where the Sun and Earth are, in case anyone ever finds it. Even if it were heading straight for Aldebaran, the trip would take it over 2 million years.

name: Pioneer 11
why: The first spacecraft to visit Saturn, it ran out of power in 1995 and is now drifting out of the solar system.
science: Pioneer 11 flew past Jupiter in 1974 and became the first spacecraft to reach Saturn in 1979, discovering a thin new ring now called the F ring.
story: I followed my twin, Pioneer 10, to Jupiter. Then Jupiter's gravity flung me all the way across the solar system to Saturn, and I became its first visitor. My power faded in 1995, and now I drift toward the constellation Aquila, the Eagle.
funFact: Pioneer 11 skimmed just 43,000 km above Jupiter's cloud tops, much closer than Pioneer 10 had gone.

name: Voyager 1
status: Still whispering home (2 science instruments on)
why: The most distant human-made object, it left the Sun's protective bubble (the heliosphere) in 2012 and still sends data from interstellar space.
science: Voyager 1 explored Jupiter and Saturn, then in 2012 became the first spacecraft to reach interstellar space. Its magnetometer and plasma-wave instrument still measure the space between the stars.
story: I'm the farthest thing people have ever built. In November 2026 I reach one light-day from Earth, so my radio messages take a whole day to get home. Engineers have switched off most of my instruments to save power, but I'm still listening to the magnetic fields and plasma waves of interstellar space.
funFact: In 1990 Voyager 1 turned its camera back and took the 'Pale Blue Dot' photo, showing Earth as a tiny speck from about 6 billion km away.

name: Voyager 2
status: Still whispering home (3 science instruments on)
why: The only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune, it entered interstellar space in 2018 and is still talking to Earth.
science: Voyager 2 flew past all four giant planets: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune, discovering new moons and rings. Its magnetometer, plasma-wave and cosmic-ray instruments still study interstellar space.
story: I launched 16 days before my twin, Voyager 1, so I'm really the older sibling! I'm the only visitor Uranus and Neptune have ever had. In 2026 my engineers swapped some power-hungry parts for thriftier ones so I can keep doing science longer.
funFact: Both Voyagers carry a Golden Record with sounds and pictures of Earth, including greetings in 55 languages.

name: New Horizons
why: After the first-ever flyby of Pluto, it is heading out of the solar system and will never come back.
science: New Horizons flew past Pluto in July 2015 and revealed a giant heart-shaped plain of nitrogen ice. In 2019 it visited Arrokoth, the most distant object ever explored up close.
story: I traveled nine and a half years to meet Pluto, zooming past it on July 14, 2015. Now I cruise through the icy Kuiper Belt. In June 2026 I woke up healthy from my longest nap yet, more than 10 months of hibernation.
funFact: New Horizons carries some of the ashes of Clyde Tombaugh, the astronomer who discovered Pluto in 1930.

name: Juno
why: Juno is still circling Jupiter. When it finally stops working, its orbit will slowly sink and it will burn up in Jupiter's atmosphere.
science: Juno studies Jupiter's deep interior, giant storms and auroras from a looping orbit over the poles. It found that Jupiter's core is 'fuzzy' and mixed rather than small and solid, and it has flown close to the moons Ganymede, Europa and Io.
story: I reached Jupiter in July 2016 and have been swooping over its poles ever since. My mission was planned to end in 2025, but I kept working into 2026. I run on sunlight, collected by three giant solar panels.
funFact: Juno carries three tiny aluminum LEGO figures: the astronomer Galileo, the god Jupiter and the goddess Juno.

name: Galileo
why: With its fuel nearly gone, NASA steered Galileo into Jupiter so it could never crash into Europa, a moon that may hide an ocean.
science: Galileo was the first spacecraft to orbit Jupiter. It found strong evidence of a salty ocean under Europa's ice and discovered that the moon Ganymede has its own magnetic field.
story: Space Shuttle Atlantis carried me into space in 1989. My big umbrella-shaped antenna got stuck and never fully opened, so engineers taught me to send my pictures home through a much smaller one. After nearly eight years orbiting Jupiter, I dove into the giant planet on purpose to protect Europa.
funFact: On the way to Jupiter, Galileo discovered the first known moon of an asteroid: tiny Dactyl, circling the asteroid Ida.

name: Galileo Probe
why: The first probe to dive into a giant planet's atmosphere, it was crushed and melted by Jupiter's heat and pressure.
science: The probe measured Jupiter's air directly for the first time. It found much less water than scientists expected and very strong winds deep below the clouds.
story: I rode on Galileo for nearly six years, then let go in July 1995. On December 7, 1995, I hit Jupiter's atmosphere at about 170,000 km/h. A parachute slowed me down, and I radioed data for about 58 minutes before the heat silenced me.
funFact: As the probe slammed into Jupiter's atmosphere, the gas around its heat shield became hotter than the surface of the Sun.

name: Cassini
why: Low on fuel, Cassini was sent into Saturn on purpose so it could never crash into the moons Enceladus or Titan, which might be able to support life.
science: Cassini spent 13 years at Saturn. It discovered geysers of water spraying from the moon Enceladus and saw lakes and seas of liquid methane on Titan.
story: I arrived at Saturn in 2004, carrying Europe's Huygens probe, which landed on Titan. For my Grand Finale I dove 22 times through the gap between Saturn and its rings. On September 15, 2017, I plunged into Saturn, sending back science until the very end.
funFact: Cassini flew right through the icy spray from Enceladus and 'tasted' it: it is salty water from an ocean hidden under the ice.

name: MESSENGER
why: After running out of fuel, MESSENGER crashed into Mercury at about 14,000 km/h, making a brand-new crater.
science: MESSENGER was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury. It found water ice hiding in permanently shadowed craters near Mercury's poles, even though Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
story: It took me six and a half years and six planet flybys to sneak into orbit around Mercury. I circled it more than 4,000 times and mapped the whole planet. When my fuel ran out, I crashed into the surface on April 30, 2015, making a crater about 16 meters wide.
funFact: MESSENGER hid behind a sunshade made of heat-proof ceramic cloth, because sunlight at Mercury can be up to 11 times stronger than on Earth.

name: Magellan
status: Burned up in Venus's sky in 1994
why: At the end of its mission, Magellan was steered deep into Venus's thick atmosphere to study it, and it burned up.
science: Magellan used radar to see through Venus's thick clouds and mapped 98% of the surface, revealing volcanoes, lava plains and craters.
story: In 1989 I became the first planetary explorer launched from a Space Shuttle. Venus hides under clouds, so I mapped it with radar, like seeing with echoes. In October 1994 I dove into its thick air on purpose and burned up.
funFact: Magellan was partly built from spare parts left over from other missions, including Voyager and Galileo.

name: Pioneer Venus Orbiter
status: Burned up in Venus's sky in 1992
why: After almost 14 years orbiting Venus, it ran out of fuel, sank into the atmosphere and burned up.
science: It made the first radar map of most of Venus's surface and studied how the solar wind strips gas from Venus's upper atmosphere.
story: I reached Venus on December 4, 1978, and kept watch for nearly 14 years. I measured Venus's clouds and upper air, and even its mountains using radar. When my fuel was gone, I slipped into the atmosphere in October 1992.
funFact: In 1986, when Halley's Comet was too close to the Sun to be seen from Earth, Pioneer Venus Orbiter watched it in ultraviolet light.

name: Pioneer Venus Large Probe
why: It parachuted into Venus's clouds and fell all the way to the scorching surface, where it stopped transmitting.
science: The Large Probe measured the gases, temperature and cloud layers of Venus's atmosphere all the way down to the ground.
story: I was the biggest of four probes dropped into Venus on December 9, 1978. I opened a parachute high in the clouds, then let it go and fell freely the rest of the way. I sent data for nearly an hour until I hit the ground.
funFact: Its body was a sealed titanium ball, built like a submarine to survive air pressure about 90 times greater than on Earth.

name: Pioneer Venus Small Probes (North, Day, Night)
why: Three identical probes dropped into different parts of Venus, and all three reached the surface, where they still lie.
science: By measuring three far-apart places at the same time, they showed how temperature and winds change across Venus.
story: We were triplets with no parachutes, named North, Day and Night for where we were aimed. None of us was built to survive landing, but Day kept sending signals from the 460-degree ground for more than an hour.
funFact: The Day Probe kept transmitting from Venus's surface for 67 minutes, even though it was never designed to land.

name: Dawn
why: Dawn ran out of the fuel it needed to point its antenna at Earth, so it is silent but still circling the dwarf planet Ceres, where it should stay for at least 20 years.
science: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit two different worlds beyond Earth: the giant asteroid Vesta and the dwarf planet Ceres. It found that Ceres's famous bright spots are salts left behind by salty water from below.
story: I used gentle ion engines, pushing with glowing xenon gas, to travel between worlds. I orbited Vesta for over a year, then flew on to Ceres in 2015. My fuel ran out in 2018, and now I silently circle Ceres like a tiny moon.
funFact: Dawn was the first spacecraft to orbit a dwarf planet: it reached Ceres in March 2015, a few months before New Horizons flew past Pluto.

name: NEAR Shoemaker
why: NEAR Shoemaker was the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid, and it is still sitting on Eros today.
science: It orbited the asteroid Eros for a year, mapping its rocky, crater-covered surface, then landed and measured what the asteroid is made of.
story: I wasn't built to land, but on February 12, 2001, my team gently set me down on Eros anyway, at about walking speed. I kept sending data from the surface for more than two weeks.
funFact: NEAR went into orbit around Eros, an asteroid named after the god of love, on Valentine's Day, February 14, 2000.

name: Kepler Space Telescope
status: Retired in 2018, trailing Earth around the Sun
why: Kepler ran out of fuel and was switched off in 2018. It keeps circling the Sun in an orbit that trails behind Earth.
science: Kepler stared at more than 150,000 stars, watching for tiny dips in light when planets passed in front of them. It discovered more than 2,600 planets and showed that our galaxy has more planets than stars.
story: For nine and a half years I watched stars dim as planets crossed in front of them. My team sent my final 'goodnight' commands on November 15, 2018. Now I follow Earth around the Sun, slowly drifting behind it.
funFact: Kepler's 'goodnight' commands were sent 388 years to the day after the death of the astronomer Johannes Kepler, the telescope's namesake.

name: Spitzer Space Telescope
status: Retired in 2020, trailing Earth around the Sun
why: NASA's infrared space telescope was switched off in 2020 and still orbits the Sun, trailing behind Earth.
science: Spitzer saw the universe in infrared (heat) light, peering through dust to find newborn stars. It helped reveal that the star TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-size planets.
story: I was designed to work for at least two and a half years, but I kept going for more than 16. I could see the heat glow of things hidden behind clouds of dust. In January 2020 I was switched off, and now I follow Earth around the Sun.
funFact: Spitzer discovered a giant, nearly invisible ring around Saturn, the biggest of all its rings, made of dust from the moon Phoebe.

name: Deep Impact Impactor
why: NASA crashed this copper-heavy impactor into comet Tempel 1 on purpose, to blast out material from inside the comet.
science: The blast showed that the comet is coated in fine, powdery dust, and it revealed water ice and carbon-rich (organic) material in the debris.
story: I rode on the Deep Impact spacecraft until the day before the crash, then flew on my own, steering myself into the comet. I hit Tempel 1 on July 4, 2005, at about 37,000 km/h, the biggest Fourth of July firework ever!
funFact: In 2011, NASA's Stardust spacecraft flew past Tempel 1 and photographed the crater that Deep Impact made.

name: Stardust
why: After dropping its comet-dust capsule back to Earth in 2006, Stardust used up its fuel in 2011 and was switched off in orbit around the Sun.
science: Stardust caught dust from comet Wild 2 in a super-light material called aerogel and brought it to Earth. Scientists found glycine, an amino acid (one of the building blocks of proteins), in the comet samples.
story: In 2004 I flew through the dusty cloud around comet Wild 2 and caught tiny grains in my aerogel 'catcher's mitt'. My capsule parachuted into the Utah desert in 2006. Then I visited a second comet, Tempel 1, before my team switched me off for good.
funFact: Stardust's capsule hit Earth's atmosphere at 12.9 km per second, the fastest re-entry of any human-made object at the time.

name: DART
why: NASA crashed DART into a small asteroid moon on purpose, to test whether we could nudge a dangerous asteroid away from Earth.
science: The crash shortened Dimorphos's orbit around its bigger partner, Didymos, by about 33 minutes. That proved that hitting an asteroid can change its path.
story: I was the world's first planetary defense test. I steered myself toward a target I could barely see until the last hour, and on September 26, 2022, I hit Dimorphos at about 22,000 km/h. Don't worry: Dimorphos was never a danger to Earth.
funFact: Europe's Hera spacecraft is due to arrive at Didymos and Dimorphos in late 2026 to study the mark DART left behind.

name: OSIRIS-REx / OSIRIS-APEX
status: Active, on its way to asteroid Apophis (arrives 2029)
why: Not abandoned yet: after delivering a sample of asteroid Bennu to Earth in 2023, the spacecraft got a new job visiting asteroid Apophis.
science: OSIRIS-REx brought back 121.6 grams of asteroid Bennu. The sample contains water-bearing minerals and organic molecules, including amino acids.
story: In 2020 I touched asteroid Bennu for just a few seconds and grabbed some of its rubble. I dropped the sample off at Earth in 2023. Then my team renamed me OSIRIS-APEX and pointed me at asteroid Apophis, which I'll meet in 2029, right after it zooms safely past Earth.
funFact: Bennu's surface was so loose that the spacecraft would have sunk into it if it had not fired its thrusters to back away right after grabbing the sample.
